svg.title: Seven row comparison of VPLS and EVPN across control plane, learning, flooding, multihoming, scalability, mobility and convergence
svg.desc: A seven row table. VPLS builds pseudowires with LDP or RSVP and learns MACs by flooding in the data plane; EVPN uses MP-BGP to carry MAC and IP addresses. VPLS floods unknown unicast and ARP heavily, multihoming is limited to MC-LAG, scalability is medium with quadratic pseudowire counts, MAC mobility is limited and convergence is slow because of re-flooding. EVPN proxies ARP, supports native all-active multihoming with ESI and designated forwarder election, scales on BGP routes with no full mesh, optimises MAC mobility with an extended community and sequence number, and converges through BGP withdraw and Ethernet auto-discovery routes. A note says the two columns differ in one dimension only: where the state lives.
svg.text: VPLS and EVPN differ in one dimension: where the forwarding state lives
Everything in the right column is a consequence of that single move from the data plane to the control plane
LDP or RSVP: builds the wire only
the same protocol family as L3VPN
the network knows before traffic arrives
one site’s storm reaches every site
BUM is bounded by the IMET tree
ESI plus DF election, every link forwards
plus MAC table pressure on every PE
no full mesh is required between PEs
then relearn at the new location
one update withdraws a whole ESI
Read the table as one sentence: VPLS asks the traffic to describe the topology, EVPN asks the topology to describe itself.
The first scales with the number of conversations; the second scales with the number of endpoints. That is why the answer changes once a domain passes a few dozen sites.
